one_liner: Statically typed game scripting language with tree interpreter, C++ AOT and LLVM JIT; interpreter outpaces Lua 5.5 and QuickJS.
what_it_does: Daslang (formerly daScript) is a statically typed scripting language from Gaijin Entertainment, embedded in a C++ host (compileDaScript, a Context, simulate, evalWithCatch) with C++ functions and types bound through addExtern/DAS_BIND_FUN and ManagedStructureAnnotation. Script data has the same layout as C++, so calls in either direction pass data without marshaling or boxing. The same script can run in a tree-based interpreter (hot reload), be translated ahead of time to C++ (for consoles and iOS, which forbid JIT), or be JIT-compiled through LLVM. It is a new language, not a drop-in for Lua or JavaScript code.
how_it_is_fast: Static typing lets the compiler build unboxed, type-specialised evaluation nodes, and the interpreter walks that tree of specialised simulation nodes (SimNode_*) directly instead of decoding bytecode with run-time type checks. Vector types such as float2 and float3 are built-in value types (the particles kernel uses a vec3_ldu hint), so vector math needs no heap objects, and host calls cost little because no data is converted. The AOT and LLVM JIT tiers reach C++ speed on the same suite (Linux fibonacci recursive: DAS JIT 0.002811 s, C++ 0.002811 s).
when_to_use: A C++ game engine or ECS that calls scripts every frame, where Lua or Squirrel marshaling costs too much: 1M host calls took 0.003740 s in the DAS interpreter vs 0.015360 s in Lua 5.5.1 on Linux.

Targets that forbid JIT (consoles, iOS): use the interpreter during development and AOT-to-C++ for shipping, with hybrid mode falling back to the interpreter for functions whose semantic hash changed.
Numeric and vector-heavy gameplay code (particles, n-body, spectral norm) that benefits from static types and SIMD value types.
Teams that want static types, hot reload (the docs cite about 5 s to recompile a full production game) and a compile-time macro system.
Desktop or server hosts that can ship LLVM, where the JIT tier gets near-C++ speed from script code.
when_not_to_use: Existing Lua or JavaScript code, or modders who expect those languages: Daslang is not source-compatible with either.

Short-lived or startup-sensitive scripts: hello world takes 0.0187 s (macOS) and 0.0261 s (Linux) in the interpreter, and 0.089 to 0.113 s under JIT, against about 0.0024 to 0.0039 s for Lua and QuickJS.

Running untrusted scripts: the language is '99% safe, not 100%', with unsafe blocks and raw pointers, and open issues include a deep recursion that kills the interpreter with SIGSEGV (#4110) and fuzzer crashes (#4101).

Small-footprint embedding: it is a large C++17 code base (23,104 commits) with submodules, and the JIT needs LLVM; the 'nano' runtime is smaller but drops the GC, string builders, the math module and threads.

Recursion- or allocation-heavy code where other interpreters are faster: on Linux LuaJIT -joff beat it on tree (0.018248 vs 0.023617 s) and fibonacci recursive (0.034842 vs 0.048174 s), and Mono --interpreter won tree on both platforms.

integration.form: static lib (libDaScript) or shared lib (libDaScriptDyn) via CMake find_package(DAS); AOT output is C++ source compiled into the host
integration.dependencies: git submodules (README build step); an LLVM shared library only for the JIT tier, which is off by default (CMake option DAS_LLVM_DISABLED defaults to ON); optional modules (dasHV, GLFW, ImGui, Vulkan, Metal) are switched by CMake options
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 and CMake 3.17+; the benchmark used Clang 19.1.7 (Linux) and AppleClang 21 (macOS); MSVC is supported
integration.platforms: Windows, Linux and macOS (x86-64 and Apple M1 in the benchmark), WebAssembly through an Emscripten build, and consoles/iOS through AOT per the design notes
integration.thread_safety: One Context per script instance holds its own globals, stack and heap; the integration notes say several standalone instances can be created and driven on any thread. Sharing one Context across threads is not documented as safe (the benchmark runner sets threadlock_context).

gotchas: Harness flaw behind the largest ratio: dasProfile's Lua sha256 sends every AND and XOR through vararg wrappers (select('#', ...) loops over closures built with load()) although Lua 5.5 has native bitwise operators, and assembles words with string.byte. The DAS kernel uses inline operators with unsafe_deref and unsafe_range_check hints and loads 32-bit words straight from memory without a byte swap; it matches the reference hash only because the 1024-byte input is all '.'. The 27x over Lua on sha256 therefore mostly measures the Lua kernel's style; the independent sashi0034 suite shows Daslang about 2.5x faster than Lua on sha256 (224.411 vs 549.956).

Mandelbrot and particles are not like-for-like either. The Lua mandelbrot (Ligneul 2017) uses metatable Complex objects that allocate several tables per iteration, and its repeat-until loop counts iterations differently, while DAS uses float2 values and QuickJS uses plain doubles. The Lua particles kernel runs 'for i = 0, count' (11 passes against DAS's 10) on nested pos/vel tables, while DAS uses SIMD float3. The 32x and 41x gaps on the Linux table shrink to about 2.4x and 2.6x in sashi0034's suite.

On like-for-like kernels the margin is small: on Linux fibonacci recursive the DAS interpreter took 0.048174 s and Lua 0.048747 s (parity; 1.55x on macOS). The clear structural win is interop host calls (about 4.1x Lua on Linux). In sashi0034's Windows suite, Lua wins sort (6.175 vs 237.142) and string2float (68.624 vs 107.174).

Open stability issues: deep recursion kills the interpreter with SIGSEGV (#4110), heap_collect frees strings that are still live (#3734), a stale .shared_module ABI mismatch crashes with SIGSEGV (#3466), and fuzzer crashes remain (#4101). The README still says the JIT needs LLVM 16.0.6 at lib/LLVM.dll, while the benchmark used LLVM 22.1.5.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Daslang over Luau, Ravi or Pallene when a C++ engine calls scripts every frame and you can adopt a new statically typed language: it avoids marshaling and has an AOT path for JIT-less consoles. Pick Luau when you need Lua compatibility and sandboxing, QuickJS when you need JavaScript, and LuaJIT Remake only for research into interpreter generation.
verified_claims_summary: borisbat/dasProfile, written by the daslang lead developer, times 16 kernels; each cell is the median of five processes, each running the kernel for a 0.5 s budget. On Linux (Ryzen 7 PRO 8700GE, Clang 19.1.7, daslang 0.6.4) the DAS interpreter beats Lua 5.5.1 and QuickJS 2026-06-04 on every kernel, from parity on fibonacci recursive (0.048174 s vs 0.048747 s vs 0.088087 s) to 27x and 8.5x on sha256 (0.002510 s vs 0.068548 s vs 0.021312 s), and the M1 Max table shows the same pattern. The largest gaps come from Lua kernels written with vararg bit-op wrappers or table-allocating complex numbers; an independent Windows suite (sashi0034, unreviewed Codex-generated code, CPU and units not stated) puts Daslang 1.4x to 3.4x ahead of Lua on 13 of 16 workloads.
status_note: Actively developed (last commit 2026-10-06, 23,104 commits) under BSD-3-Clause and built for Gaijin's ECS game engine per its design notes; a large and fast-moving code base with open crash issues, so pin a release such as 0.6.4.
